Senses.Explanation: An emphatic warning governing an action or error: literally 'urgently avoid,' hence 'strictly avoid,' 'take care not to,' or 'beware of.' The object supplied by the record must be translated rather than replaced by a general spiritual warning. Daowu says, 'where knowledge does not reach, strictly avoid speaking of it' (智不到處，切忌道著); Daoqian answers a question about words that display the Way with 'strictly avoid choosing' (切忌揀擇); Tianyin tells the assembly 'strictly avoid conjecturing' (切忌卜度). Other high-seat warnings preserve concrete allusions: 'the sword has long gone; strictly avoid marking the boat' (劍去久矣，切忌刻舟), and 'if you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, beware being branded on the forehead' (不是龍門客，切忌遭點額). Its Chan use is a direct warning embedded in interviews and public addresses, not a commentator's private aside.

Outline Record of the Successive Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄): The Record of Guiding Principles of the Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄), under the explicit Yu'an Ji heading for entering Longjiao Monastery, records Yu'an pairing the buddha's appearance with transmitting error and Bodhidharma's arrival with following error by error.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不將錯就錯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB163.xml). Selected Record of Chan Master Guting’s Sayings (古庭禪師語錄輯略): The Abridged Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guting (古庭禪師語錄輯略), in Guting Shanjian's instruction, records him saying that Zhaozhou did not follow error with error while even the great canon does not go outside it.

Senses.Explanation: To follow one error with another is to proceed from an already mistaken position by means of a further mistake. Gunanmen says Shakyamuni, pressed until no route of retreat remained, could only do this; Zhongfeng Mingben warns his assembly not to do it while asking who can speak for Linji; Sanshan Denglai issues the phrase as a verdict when an unnamed monk bows and withdraws. Tiebi Huiji asks what the error is and answers with eating tea or rice when each comes, while Jie Weizhou rejects preserving faulty writing under this excuse. Guting Shanjian can even prohibit the phrase while discussing Zhaozhou. Warning, case comment, and interview verdict differ in stance toward the same act, not in the phrase's sense.

Senses.Explanation: Pointing to a deer and calling it a horse is a verdict for false identification. Chan masters apply the old idiom to asserted understanding, inherited formulations, and verbal performance that names one thing as another while claiming to present the matter. Zhongfeng Mingben rejects a proposed ‘formless true person’ as pointing to a deer and calling it a horse. Baoning Yuanji applies the same verdict to advice to seek only within oneself, refusing the inherited identification. Opening addresses, verse admonitions, and anthology comments reuse the idiom against misnaming teachings and performances. The corpus supplies the inference directly: the fault is calling one presented thing by another name.

Senses.Explanation: “Pass a ladder to a thief” (與賊過梯) describes furnishing the means by which a thief advances. Gunan uses the verdict on Cuiyan’s and Xuedou’s handling of an exchange. Zhihai says any unchecked speech passes a ladder to a thief, then announces that he has caught the assembly together with the stolen goods. A preface stages an anonymous objection that publishing models might do this, then has its author reject that charge; Jiangshan applies the phrase to an appraisal of Deshan; Jinshan uses it against a reading of the Third Patriarch. The corpus thus records the phrase as a criticism of giving an opponent, imitator, or disputed reading its next foothold.
